Title: fix: avoid IndexError in is_mostly_bin for short tails

fixes [ref].

reproducible with any bytes payload of len 101–103 where index 100 is a UTF-8 continuation byte:

```python
>>> from mitmproxy.utils import strutils
>>> strutils.is_mostly_bin(b'a' * 100 + b'\x80')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
IndexError: index out of range
```

the lookahead loop `range(100, 104)` reads `s[100]` through `s[103]` to find the start of the next UTF-8 char and avoid chopping a multibyte code point in half. when len(s) is between 101 and 103 and the first byte past the 100-byte cutoff is a continuation byte, the loop continues into out-of-range indices.

cap the loop end at `len(s)`. the existing `s[:100]` fallback still covers the case where every byte in the lookahead window is a continuation byte.

added a small regression assertion for the three affected lengths.
tasks.goldTitle: fix: avoid IndexError in is_mostly_bin for short tails

Title: Copy issuer's SubjectKeyIdentifier into leaf AuthorityKeyIdentifier (RFC 5280 §4.2.1.2)

#### Description

`[path]::dummy_cert` builds the leaf certificate's `AuthorityKeyIdentifier` with:

```python
x509.AuthorityKeyIdentifier.from_issuer_public_key(cacert.public_key())
```

`cryptography`'s `from_issuer_public_key` always derives the keyIdentifier as the **SHA-1** of the issuer's BIT STRING public key. It ignores whatever `SubjectKeyIdentifier` the issuer cert actually has stored. This violates RFC 5280 §4.2.1.2:

> The value of the subject key identifier MUST be the value placed in the key identifier field of the authority key identifier extension of certificates issued by the subject of this certificate.

It also makes mitmproxy incompatible with any CA whose stored SKI was not derived as SHA-1 — an entirely legal choice per RFC 7093 (truncated SHA-256/384/512) and RFC 5280 (any unique value).

Strict TLS chain builders (`X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT`, Python `ssl`, Go `crypto/x509`, modern Java) all use AKI to find the issuer candidate during chain construction, so an AKI/SKI mismatch is rejected with `authority and subject key identifier mismatch` — even though the issuer's subject DN matches and the signature verifies.

##### Why this is hitting more users now

- **cert-manager ≥ 1.18** (Oct 2025) defaults to truncated SHA-256 SKIs for FIPS 140-3 compliance. Any mitmproxy deployment whose CA was provisioned by cert-manager (very common in Kubernetes egress / corporate intercept setups) breaks.
- **Go ≥ 1.25** (Aug 2025) does the same when generating self-signed CAs (`GODEBUG=x509sha256skid=1`, on by default). Tools that wrap Go's `crypto/x509` to produce CAs (cert-manager being one) inherit this.
- Hand-rolled CAs with `subjectKeyIdentifier=hash:sha256` in the OpenSSL config trigger it too.

The closest existing report is [ref], which was closed without investigation after the OP misdiagnosed it as a CA-trust-store problem.

##### Reproduction

```bash
# 1) Make a CA with a non-SHA-1 SKI (mimics cert-manager output).
cat > /tmp/ca.cnf <<'CNF'
[req]
distinguished_name = req
x509_extensions    = v3_ca
prompt             = no
CN                 = Test CA
[v3_ca]
basicConstraints       = critical,CA:TRUE
keyUsage               = critical,keyCertSign,cRLSign
subjectKeyIdentifier   = hash:sha256
CNF
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 3650 \
  -keyout /tmp/ca.key -out /tmp/ca.crt -config /tmp/ca.cnf

# 2) Hand it to mitmproxy as the CA.
cat /tmp/ca.crt /tmp/ca.key > ~/.mitmproxy/mitmproxy-ca.pem
mitmdump -p 8080 &

# 3) Trust /tmp/ca.crt system-wide, then:
curl --proxy [ref] [ref]
# curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: authority and subject key identifier mismatch
```

##### Fix

Prefer the issuer's stored SKI verbatim, falling back to the previous SHA-1-of-public-key behavior only when the issuer has no `SubjectKeyIdentifier` extension at all. The change is fully backward-compatible: when the issuer cert was generated by mitmproxy itself (or any other tool that does in fact use SHA-1 of the public key for the SKI), `from_issuer_subject_key_identifier(stored_ski)` and `from_issuer_public_key(public_key)` produce byte-identical results.

##### Tests

Added two regression tests in `[path]::TestDummyCert`:

- `test_aki_copies_issuer_ski_non_sha1` — builds a CA whose stored SKI is a truncated SHA-256 (as cert-manager / Go 1.25+ would produce) and asserts the leaf's AKI is byte-equal to the CA's stored SKI.
- `test_aki_falls_back_when_issuer_has_no_ski` — pins the legacy fallback path: if the CA has no SKI extension, the leaf's AKI is still computed from the issuer's public key and matches the prior behavior.

All existing `[module]` tests pass (36 total). I also re-ran `[path]` to make sure nothing downstream of `dummy_cert` was affected (62 tests total, all pass). `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, and `mypy [path]` are clean.

##### Verification with real clients

Outside the unit tests I also reproduced the bug end-to-end on a Kubernetes minikube cluster with a cert-manager-issued CA, then re-ran the same tests with a `mitmweb` instance whose `dummy_cert` had been runtime-patched with this same change. Strict TLS chain validation through Python `requests`, Go `net/http`, and `curl --cacert` all flipped from `authority and subject key identifier mismatch` to a successful intercept, with no other code changes.
tasks.goldTitle: Copy issuer's SubjectKeyIdentifier into leaf AuthorityKeyIdentifier (RFC 5280 §4.2.1.2)

Title: mitmweb: honor view_order_reversed for live flows

Fixes [ref].

## Problem

In mitmweb the `view_order_reversed` option only affected the initial flow list. Flows that arrive afterwards over the WebSocket were always appended to the bottom of the table, so enabling the option did not keep the newest flow visible at the top. This is the behaviour reported in the issue, and it matches what Prinzhorn observed there (the option is ignored and new rows are appended).

## Cause

The initial `/flows` response is sent in the server view order, which already respects `view_order_reversed`, and the client keeps that order when no column sort is active. Live `flows/add` events go through `insertViewItem` instead, and with no active column sort the comparator is a no-op, so `findInsertPos` always returns the end of the list. The client never consulted `view_order_reversed`.

## Change

The flows reducer now tracks `view_order_reversed` from the options state. When no column sort is active, a newly added flow is inserted at the front if the option is set and at the back otherwise, which is the same order the server uses for the initial list. An active column sort still takes precedence and is unchanged.

The fix is limited to newly added flows, which are unambiguously the most recent. The order restored when a column sort is toggled back off is left as it was.

## Tests

Added reducer tests covering the option being read from `OPTIONS_RECEIVE` and `OPTIONS_UPDATE`, front insertion when reversed, back insertion when not, and a column sort taking precedence over the option. `npm test` (eslint, tsc, jest) passes locally.
tasks.goldTitle: mitmweb: honor view_order_reversed for live flows

Title: net.tls: handle SSL.Error from set_min/max_proto_version in is_supported_version

## Description

`mitmproxy.net.tls.is_supported_version()` builds an `SSL.Context`, sets the
min/max protocol version, then probes support with `client_conn.recv()`. Only
the `recv()` probe was wrapped in `try/except SSL.Error`.

On OpenSSL builds that have dropped a protocol version entirely (e.g. SSLv3
after POODLE / CVE-2014-3566, see pyca/cryptography[ref]),
`set_min_proto_version(SSL3_VERSION)` raises `SSL.Error` immediately at
context-setup time — *before* the guarded `recv()`. The exception then
propagated unhandled and crashed callers. The only production caller,
`TlsConfig._warn_unsupported_version`, iterates over every `Version` to build
the "supported versions" list, so on those builds option validation crashed
outright.

This moves the protocol-version setters and connection setup inside the
existing `try`, so a setup-time `SSL.Error` is treated the same as a
probe-time one: the version is reported as unsupported (`return False`) instead
of raising. Behavior for currently-supported versions is unchanged.

A regression test (`test_supported_setup_error`) monkeypatches
`SSL.Context.set_min_proto_version` to raise `SSL.Error`, reproducing the crash
path deterministically on any OpenSSL build (the existing `test_supported[SSL3]`
only exercises the `recv()` path on builds that still allow SSL3 context setup).

Closes [ref]

Note: [ref] also touches this function but bundles it with an unrelated CRLF
prettifier fix ([ref]) across four files. This PR is a focused, single-concern
alternative scoped to [ref] only; happy to defer to whichever the maintainers
prefer.
tasks.goldTitle: net.tls: handle SSL.Error from set_min/max_proto_version in is_supported_version

Title: Don't stall QUIC flows when host ignoring is enabled

If allow_hosts or ignore_hosts was set, any QUIC connections would stall forever after TLS handshake and never get assigned an HttpLayer or e.g. appear in the flow list in mitmweb. The codepath goes like this:

1. After client TLS handshake completes, next layer hook is invoked with data_client = b'', i.e. the data so far inside the QUIC stream
2. _next_layer first checks using _ignore_connection
3. _ignore_connection uses _get_client_hello, passing b'' data_client
4. quick_parse_client_hello_from_datagram raises a type of ValueError because b'' is definitely not a valid QUIC packet
5. ValueError is skipped, so dtls_parse_client_hello is tried, which also raises a type of ValueError for about the same reason
6. This is now converted into NeedsMoreData, which bails out of the entire _next_layer process.

This repeats each time next_layer is called and never makes progress, even if data is read on the QUIC stream, it's still not going to be a valid QUIC or DTLS packet.

This fix matches the tcp case and only tries to parse the packet as quic or dtls if it heuristically looks like that.
tasks.goldTitle: Don't stall QUIC flows when host ignoring is enabled

Title: proxy: bracket IPv6 literals in upstream CONNECT authority

#### Description

In `--mode upstream`, when the target server is an IPv6 literal, the `CONNECT`
request (and `Host` header) sent to the upstream proxy was built as
`host:port` without bracketing the IPv6 address — e.g.
`CONNECT 2001:db8::1:443` / `Host: 2001:db8::1:443`. Per RFC 3986 §3.2.2 and
RFC 7230 §5.4, an IPv6 literal in an authority must be wrapped in square
brackets, so downstream proxies (e.g. Burp) reject the unbracketed form as a
malformed CONNECT target.

This brackets IPv6 literals so the authority becomes `[2001:db8::1]:443`.
Hostnames (still IDNA-encoded) and IPv4 addresses are unchanged. The same
`authority` value feeds both the request target and the `Host` header, so a
single change fixes both.

Added a regression test `test_upstream_proxy_ipv6` that drives
`HTTPMode.upstream` with an IPv6 target and asserts the outgoing `CONNECT` /
`Host` are bracketed; it fails against the previous code and passes with the
fix. The existing `test_upstream_proxy` (hostname / IDNA / IPv4) stays green.

Closes [ref]
tasks.goldTitle: proxy: bracket IPv6 literals in upstream CONNECT authority
